questions.question: When a triangle is divided by one internal line from a vertex to the opposite side, how many total triangles are formed?
questions.rationale: The one internal line creates 2 smaller triangles, plus the original outer triangle itself still counts, giving 3 total.

questions.question: What does 'triangle counting strategy' generally recommend?
options: Only count the outer triangle
Count triangles in a random order
Systematically count basic (undivided) triangles first, then count composite triangles formed by combining adjacent basic triangles
Ignore any triangle that shares an edge with another
questions.rationale: The recommended strategy counts basic triangles first, then works up to composite (combined) triangles built from adjacent basic ones.

questions.question: What is an 'inverted triangle' in a triangular grid?
options: A triangle with no valid boundary
A triangle that points in the opposite direction to the main/outer triangle
A triangle formed only by diagonals
A triangle counted twice by mistake
questions.rationale: In a triangular grid, some smaller triangles point 'upright' like the outer triangle, while others point 'inverted' (upside down) — both must be counted.

questions.question: What does an 'orientation chart' help track when counting triangles in a complex figure?
options: The color of each triangle
The order in which triangles were drawn
The exact coordinates of each vertex
Which direction (upright or inverted) each triangle points, since it's easy to miss inverted ones by visual scanning alone
questions.rationale: An orientation chart tracks each triangle's pointing direction, helping catch inverted triangles that are easy to overlook during a purely visual scan.

questions.question: What is the 'composite triangle rule'?
options: A larger triangle is valid to count only if all the smaller triangles/lines needed to form its complete boundary are actually present in the figure
Composite triangles are never valid
Composite triangles must always be inverted
Composite triangles don't require any boundary lines
questions.rationale: A composite (combined) triangle only counts if its entire boundary is genuinely present in the figure — not just visually implied.

questions.question: What must be true for a set of line segments to correctly form a valid quadrilateral when counting?
options: They must all be the same length
They must all be diagonals
The four segments must form a fully closed four-sided boundary with no gaps
They must intersect at a single point
questions.rationale: A valid quadrilateral requires four segments that together form a completely closed boundary, with no gap anywhere along its perimeter.

questions.question: What is the general strategy recommended for 'counting polygons' of a given type in a complex figure?
options: Guess based on the figure's overall size
Identify the basic units first, then systematically combine adjacent units while validating that each combination forms a genuinely closed polygon
Only count polygons with an even number of sides
Count every possible combination of lines, regardless of whether they close
questions.rationale: The same basic-then-composite strategy applies: identify basic units, then systematically test valid combinations while confirming each one actually forms a closed polygon.

questions.question: When counting line segments 'in a grid' rather than on a single line, what additional factor must be considered?
options: Nothing changes compared to a single line
Segments can run horizontally, vertically, and sometimes diagonally, so each direction must be counted separately
Only horizontal segments exist in a grid
Grids never contain more than one segment
questions.rationale: Unlike points on a single line, a grid has segments running in multiple directions (horizontal, vertical, sometimes diagonal), each of which needs its own count.

questions.question: What does the 'multiple-line segment method' address?
options: Counting segments on a single isolated line only
Counting all possible segments when there are several lines that may intersect and create additional segment combinations
Removing all diagonal segments from consideration
Only counting the longest segment in the figure
questions.rationale: This method handles the more complex case of multiple, possibly-intersecting lines, where additional segment combinations arise from the intersections.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of intersection points formed by n lines, no two parallel and no three meeting at a single point?
options: n
2n
questions.rationale: This is the same 'choose 2' logic as the line-segment formula: each pair of lines contributes exactly one intersection point, giving C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2.
